Build an LLM automation workflow with Make

Architecture · concept-level steps · cost per 1,000 runs

The problem: repetitive weekly text tasks (summarizing form feedback, tagging new articles, drafting replies) deserve automation, but "how much will the API cost per month afterwards" is often overlooked. What this article is: a generic architecture and concept-level steps for calling LLM APIs from a Make-style visual iPaaS, plus a clear per-run cost computed from this site's verified model prices. This article is documentation research (interface details follow Make's official documentation); no hands-on interface testing was performed.

1. Workflow architecture (five parts)

1. Trigger: a schedule (cron) or an event (new email, new form row, webhook) starts one execution;
2. Data preparation: fetch the content to process and trim it to the length the model needs — this step directly determines input-token cost;
3. Call the LLM API: send a request to the model endpoint through the platform's HTTP module (Bearer key authentication, JSON body); Make offers a REST-style open API and a custom-app mechanism, and most administrative endpoints require a paid subscription (per official documentation);
4. Parse and validate: check the response is usable (timeouts, rate limits, empty responses) and decide retry or fallback;
5. Follow-up actions: write back to a sheet, send a notification, update a ticket.

Cost control lives in steps 2 and 4: longer inputs and more retries mean higher bills. Unit and cache prices per model are in the table below.

2. Concept-level steps (not a click-by-click tutorial)

1. Create a new Scenario on the platform and configure the trigger's schedule;
2. Add a data-fetching module (read the form / email / file) and trim fields with length truncation;
3. Add an HTTP module: POST to the model endpoint, authentication in the headers, body = {model, input, parameters};
4. Configure error handling: bounded retries with backoff for 429/5xx, and defaults for empty responses;
5. Trial with a small volume first, record the actual input/output tokens per execution, then estimate the monthly bill with the cost table below;
6. Set platform-side alerts (consecutive failures) so a broken flow fails loudly instead of silently burning quota.

Buttons, module names and billing details change with platform versions; this article deliberately stays at the concept level. Follow Make's official documentation and your actual console.

Assume each workflow run makes one model call (2,000 input / 800 output tokens, 30% cache hit rate, off-peak rates). The table below shows the LLM API cost per 1,000 runs, computed from official list prices by this site's build script:

Replace the per-call input/output tokens with the real values from your trial and recompute in the cost calculator; note this is the API-side cost only — platform-side charges by operation count are covered in the next section.

4. Platform-side cost and retry amplification (run the numbers twice)

· Two bills: total cost = platform operation fees + LLM API fees. The former depends on the platform plan and modules consumed per execution — current Make and n8n pricing has not been verified by this site; check each vendor's official site. This article cites no unverified price numbers;
· Retry amplification: if each task retries 0.5 times on average, real API consumption ×1.5; under heavy rate limiting it is worse. Write retry caps, backoff and "fail to manual review" into the flow before shopping for a cheaper model;
· Input trimming: cutting a 20,000-token source to 2,000 tokens at step 2 cuts input cost by an order of magnitude — the most certain optimization in automation scenarios.

5. When not to choose Make

If data must not leave your intranet, choose a self-hostable option such as n8n — a fair-code licensed tool with Docker self-hosting support (see the n8n documentation); if the flow is highly customized and needs code-level control, build a custom API; at very high execution volumes with an ops team, self-hosting is usually cheapest — but rate limiting, retries and monitoring become your own job. The comparison framework across the three options is in Make, n8n or a custom API — neither article contains any promotional links.
